cf.title: Improve hash aggregate spilling by writing only the needed columns

input.subject: Improve hash aggregate spilling by writing only the needed columns

verdict_reasoning: No objection survived at levels 1a, 1b or 2. The problem and the design are stated in message #1, the cost falls only on executions that spill, and two reviewers reproduced the gains. The earlier planner-side attempt [P3] was reverted for a regression that this executor-side design avoids. Confidence is medium because the code was not read and no committer has spoken in the visible thread.

brief.title: Write only the needed columns to hash aggregate spill files
brief.problem: Hash aggregate spills tuples using the full outer plan tuple descriptor, with unneeded columns set to NULL. When a seq scan passes whole table tuples, wide tables make the aggregate write and read much more spill data than it uses. This affects analytic queries such as TPC-H Q18.
brief.proposed_design: On the first spill, nodeAgg builds a compact tuple descriptor with only the needed columns and a map back to the input layout. The write path gathers needed values into the compact slot, and the read path scatters them back into the input tuple layout. A tuple read from a spill file that must spill again is written as read, without deform and form.
author_claims: TPC-H Q18 at SF5 and SF10 runs about 24% faster and spills about 21-23% less, with work_mem = 4MB.
No behaviour change when all input columns are needed.
No cost for executions that never spill, after the deferred initialization in v2.
Reviewer Alain Lesage reports a -38% geometric mean on the 14 spilling ClickBench queries.
brief.thread_state: Three reviewers replied. Xiaoxuan Li found a JIT crash with grouping sets from a stale FIELDNO_AGGSTATE_ALL_PERGROUPS, fixed in v2 together with the deferred initialization that Ethan Tran suggested, and Alain Lesage confirmed both fixes and the gains on v2.
unclear: The patch adds no regression tests, and v2 does not say whether it adds any for sparse columns, respill, grouping sets or the JIT case.
Ethan's request for a comment on Datum ownership between the compact slot and the input slot has no visible answer.
The thread does not say how tuples are handled when the input slot is not a heap or minimal tuple slot.
Queries that group on expressions see no gain because the scan already projects; the commit message does not mention it.

prior_attempts.title: Revert "Use CP_SMALL_TLIST for hash aggregate"
prior_attempts.quote: This reverts commit 4cad2534da6d17067d98cf04be2dfc1bda8f2cd0 due to a performance regression.
prior_attempts.reason:
This reverts commit 4cad2534da6d17067d98cf04be2dfc1bda8f2cd0 due to a
performance regression. It will be replaced by a new approach in an
upcoming commit.
prior_attempts.what_is_different: P3 narrowed the hash aggregate input in the planner with CP_SMALL_TLIST, so every hash aggregate paid for the projection. This patch leaves the planner and the scan unchanged and narrows tuples only inside nodeAgg, on the first spill.

touch_points.label: ABI / extension API
touch_points.reason: The patch adds fields to AggState in execnodes.h, which shifts struct offsets and the JIT field number FIELDNO_AGGSTATE_ALL_PERGROUPS.

touch_points.label: maintenance burden ("who maintains this in 10 years")
touch_points.reason: nodeAgg.c gains a second spill tuple layout, a column map and a direct respill path, with no regression tests so far.

touch_points.label: performance on the hot path
touch_points.reason: The patch changes spill code reached from lookup_hash_entries(), which runs for every input tuple; hashagg_spill_tuple() is marked pg_noinline for that reason.

touch_points.label: doesn't fit what Postgres is about (extension / external tool / already solved)

questions: Does v2 add regression tests for sparse-column reconstruction, respill, grouping sets with spilling, rescans and the JIT case from message #3?
How does the write path handle an input slot that is neither a heap tuple slot nor a minimal tuple slot?
How long do the Datums that the reconstructed input slot borrows from the compact spill slot stay valid, and where does the code document that?
Will the commit message say that queries grouping on expressions see no gain because the scan already projects?

committability.owner_note: Someone who knows the executor's hash aggregate spill code in nodeAgg.c and the JIT type synchronization rule for AggState.
committability.liability: The owner signs for the correctness of the compact spill layout, the column map and the direct respill path in every later release. Spill files are temporary, so there is no on-disk or upgrade commitment.
committability.author_follow_up: The author posted v2 with the JIT fix from message #3 and the deferred initialization from message #2, which shows response to review.

priority.reason: The patch is about 10 KiB in two files, adds no user-visible surface, and shows about 24% on TPC-H Q18 and a reviewer-reported -38% geometric mean on spilling ClickBench queries. It helps analytic queries on wide tables that spill, and it needs regression tests and a committer who knows nodeAgg.

provisional_note: The code was not read, so the handling of input slot types, Datum ownership between the compact slot and the input slot, and memory context use on rescan could not be checked. Test coverage in v2 is unknown.
disclosure: Prepared by an AI harness; treat as a devil's advocate, not a verdict.

precedents_retrieved.title: Table AM modifications to accept column projection lists
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch changes the table AM API so that sequential scans, index scans, tuple_lock and tuple fetch take a column projection set, so that columnar AMs such as Zedstore read only the columns a query needs. The planner and executor collect these sets, for example scanCols and returningCols in RangeTblEntry, with separate sets for RETURNING, EPQ checks and ON CONFLICT UPDATE.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The authors withdrew the patch. They said it was hard to review in its current form and that no concrete implementation of the new API existed in core, and they had no time to improve it before the July commitfest. Reviewers had raised smaller points, such as adding scan_begin_with_column_projection as a new callback instead of extending scan_begin, but nobody objected to the design.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
We agree that
it's fairly difficult to review in its current state, and the lack of a
concrete implementation of the new API isn't helping.

precedents_retrieved.title: explain to report bucket and memory stats for TupleHashTable nodes
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds bucket counts and peak memory statistics to explain analyze output for nodes that use a TupleHashTable, such as HashAggregate, HashSetOp and Bitmap Heap Scan. It also splits memory accounting into separate contexts for the hashtable and the tuples.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The hash spill to disk commit (1f39bce02) already added most of the instrumentation, and the author asked whether the patch still served a purpose. Jeff Davis said the extra detail should go under VERBOSE or a new explain option. The patch then stayed Waiting on Author from March, and Daniel Gustafsson closed the entry when no new activity followed.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
This thread has stalled and the patch has been Waiting on Author since March,
and skimming the thread there seems to be questions raised over the value
proposition.

precedents_retrieved.title: Memory-bounded HashAgg
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch lets HashAgg spill to disk so it stays within work_mem even when the planner underestimates the number of groups. When memory is full, existing groups keep aggregating, tuples for new groups go to partition files, and each file is processed in a later pass. A GUC, enable_hashagg_disk, lets the planner choose HashAgg even when it expects the hash table to exceed memory.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The visible messages do not show why. Tomas Vondra argued for hashjoin-like batching and noted that growing transition states such as array_agg are not handled, but in message #38 he called the approach reasonable. The last message says the discussion moved to another thread.

precedents_retrieved.title: Deletion of the recycled future WAL files to free-up disk space if max_wal_size is reduced or wal_recycle is set to off
precedents_retrieved.summary: When max_wal_size is reduced or wal_recycle is set to off, a checkpoint should delete recycled future WAL files to free disk space. The author suggested keeping recycled WAL files in a sorted list and, at checkpoint, deleting them from the newest end, rebuilding the list after restart if needed.
precedents_retrieved.objection: No patch was ever posted, so the commitfest entry had nothing to review. Jacob Champion closed it for that reason and invited the author to reopen it if a patch existed. Justin Pryzby supported the idea, and Tom Lane questioned only whether the behaviour was real.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
(This is registered in CF, but there doesn't seem to be a patch as part
of this thread, so I don't think there's anything to review.

precedents_retrieved.title: Partial aggregates push down
precedents_retrieved.summary: postgres_fdw pushes partial aggregation to the remote server for aggregates marked safe by a new pg_aggregate flag (set for min/max/sum/count). For aggregates with internal state, a new converter function runs locally and turns the remote aggregate result into the local partial-aggregate state.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tomas Vondra was still not convinced of the approach in the last review. He saw no clear path to aggregates with complex states such as avg(), and he doubted that the aggpartialpushdownsafe flag without version checks ensures the remote node represents the state the same way. The author agreed he did not know how to handle complex states, and postgres_fdw has no way to learn the remote server version at planning time. The visible messages do not show further discussion before the entry was returned.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
1) It's not clear to me how could this get extended to aggregates with
more complex aggregate states, to support e.g. avg() and similar fairly
common aggregates.

precedents_retrieved.title: Memory accounting towards memory-bounded HashAgg
precedents_retrieved.summary: Jeff Davis proposed tracking allocated memory blocks per memory context, optionally including child contexts, as a base for a memory-bounded HashAgg that can spill to disk. Later versions dropped inheritance and kept only a per-context counter of blocks held, reviewed together with the disk-based HashAgg patch.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Michael Paquier returned it with feedback because the patch was "not there yet" after Tomas Vondra's review. Tomas showed that HashAgg read memory from hashcontext, so by-reference transition states in aggcontext, such as array_agg, were not counted. Measuring aggcontext correctly made a 100-group query about 2 times slower. Earlier reviews reported allocation overhead and an unresolved design question about child contexts.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
Hmm. It seems that this patch is not there yet, so marking it as
returned with feedback, especially knowing that the patch is incorrect
by using hascontext as mentioned by Tomas.

precedents_retrieved.title: Allow build.pl just to construct project files without running a build
precedents_retrieved.summary: Add an option to src/tools/msvc/build.pl so that it only generates the MSVC project files and stops before building. The author wanted this for a buildfarm recipe that runs on Appveyor without changing the Postgres source.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Heikki Linnakangas pointed out that src/tools/msvc/mkvcbuild.pl already generates the project files without building. The author agreed that it does about the same thing and withdrew the patch.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
There's already a separate script for this, src/tools/msvc/mkvcbuild.pl.
Doesn't that do the same thing?

precedents_retrieved.title: Memory Accounting (towards memory-bounded HashAgg)
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds a per-context counter of malloc'd block memory to MemoryContextData, kept current in the memory context code, plus MemoryContextMemAllocated() to read it for one context or sum it over child contexts. It is meant as groundwork for a later HashAgg patch that bounds memory and spills to disk.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Reviewers objected to adding overhead to hot paths such as AllocSetAlloc for every user, given a reported 1-3% REINDEX slowdown on a POWER machine. Tom Lane also said HashAgg could track its own memory, and that the mechanism had no use in core yet. Following Robert Haas's view that HashAgg should do its own accounting, as tuplesort.c does, Jeff Davis dropped the patch and moved the work into the HashAgg patch.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: But I think when it comes to these very hot code paths, extreme conservatism is warranted.

precedents_retrieved.title: In INSERT/UPDATE, use the table's real tuple descriptor as target.
precedents_retrieved.summary:
In INSERT/UPDATE, use the table's real tuple descriptor as target.
Reverted commit(s): Fix corner case for a BEFORE ROW UPDATE trigger returning OLD.
precedents_retrieved.objection:
Previously, ExecInitModifyTable relied on ExecInitJunkFilter,
and thence ExecCleanTypeFromTL, to build the target descriptor from
the query tlist.  While we just checked (in ExecCheckPlanOutput)
that the tlist produces compatible output, this is not a great
substitute for the relation's actual tuple descriptor that's
available from the relcache.  For one thing, dropped columns will
not be correctly marked attisdropped; it's a bit surprising that
we've gotten away with that this long.  But the real reason for
being concerned with this is that using the table's descriptor means
that the slot will have correct attrmissing data, allowing us to
revert the klugy fix of commit ba9f18abd.  (This commit undoes
that one's changes in trigger.c, but keeps the new test case.)
Thus we can solve the bogus-trigger-tuple problem with fewer cycles
rather than more.

No back-patch, since this doesn't fix any additional bug, and it
seems somewhat more likely to have unforeseen side effects than
ba9f18abd's narrow fix.

precedents_retrieved.title: Fix index-only scan plans, take 2.
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Fix index-only scan plans, take 2.
Reverted commit(s): Fix index-only scan plans when not all index columns can be returned.
precedents_retrieved.objection:
Commit 4ace45677 failed to fix the problem fully, because the
same issue of attempting to fetch a non-returnable index column
can occur when rechecking the indexqual after using a lossy index
operator.  Moreover, it broke EXPLAIN for such indexquals (which
indicates a gap in our test cases :-().

Revert the code changes of 4ace45677 in favor of adding a new field
to struct IndexOnlyScan, containing a version of the indexqual that
can be executed against the index-returned tuple without using any
non-returnable columns.  (The restrictions imposed by check_index_only
guarantee this is possible, although we may have to recompute indexed
expressions.)  Support construction of that during setrefs.c
processing by marking IndexOnlyScan.indextlist entries as resjunk
if they can't be returned, rather than removing them entirely.
(We could alternatively require setrefs.c to look up the IndexOptInfo
again, but abusing resjunk this way seems like a reasonably safe way
to avoid needing to do that.)

This solution isn't great from an API-stability standpoint: if there
are any extensions out there that build IndexOnlyScan structs directly,
they'll be broken in the next minor releases.  However, only a very
invasive extension would be likely to do such a thing.  There's no
change in the Path representation, so typical planner extensions
shouldn't have a problem.

As before, back-patch to all supported branches.

precedents_retrieved.authors: Haozhou Wang (hawang), Hubert Zhang (hubertz), Hao Wu (hwu)

roaster_notes.note: The only precedent is [P3], reverted for a performance regression. In that design every hash aggregate projected in the planner, so all of them paid, not only the ones that spill. This patch puts the cost only on the spill path, and messages #2 and #5 measured no overhead when nothing spills. Message #1 cites two earlier discussions of the same goal. The thread reports that they led to today's behaviour of setting unneeded columns to NULL, and the proposal does not say the new approach repeats what failed there.

The patch changes only the private spill file format inside nodeAgg. It adds no SQL syntax, GUC, catalog object, psql behaviour or dump content. Spill files are temporary and never cross an upgrade or reach a client. Query results and plans stay the same, and EXPLAIN output changes only in reported disk usage. From the standards and compatibility angle, there is no user-facing contract to object to. [P3] was a planner-side tlist change reverted for a performance regression, so its recorded reason does not apply here.

The patch changes only the format of temporary hash aggregate spill files, which live for one query in one backend and are never read after a crash, by a standby, by pg_upgrade or by another node, so there is no on-disk, WAL, catalog or wire protocol concern. The new AggState field in execnodes.h shifts struct offsets, but this is a master-only change; the JIT field number was fixed in v2 (message #4) and confirmed in message #5.

The proposal changes only the internal format of hash aggregate spill files inside one executor node. It adds no SQL surface, privilege, setting or monitoring output, and spill files stay private to the backend, so there is no new privilege or exposure aspect to object to. Spill disk use goes down, so the existing temp_file_limit and work_mem limits on disk use by unprivileged users still apply as before.

From the maintenance and fit angle there is no objection to raise. The change stays inside nodeAgg.c, spill files are temporary with no on-disk or upgrade commitment, there is no user-visible surface, and v2 measured no cost when nothing spills (messages #2, #4, #5). [P3] reverted a planner-side approach for a regression; this executor-side design avoids that path. Committability notes: no committer has engaged in the visible thread. The JIT field-number trap in message #3 is an existing rule, but the absence of regression tests leaves that trap and the respill path without coverage.

No existing feature, setting or extension writes only the needed columns to hash aggregate spill files, and users cannot make a plain seq scan project for the aggregate. The patch extends the current NULL-out spill path in nodeAgg; the planner-side alternative was reverted for a regression [P3], and this proposal stays inside the executor.

The demand looks real. Wide-table analytic aggregates that spill are common, and the gains show up on TPC-H Q18 and on 14 spilling ClickBench queries reproduced independently in message #5. The change adds no user-visible surface, and the cost is confined to nodeAgg spill code.
